title: Raytracing experiment with ThreeJS. built with Pixelfork (No Engine)
author: gamesformygirlfriend
selftext:
Hey everyone, 

Just wanted to try if I can achieve raytracing with AI and ThreeJS. tried it on Pixelfork. added some PBR textures there. and bullet hole decal effects, AI generated pistol model, and bullet fume effect.   
  
and just wow. I was not expecting that it would generate this reflection. Result is very impressive for me. 

NOTE: This is not a game. Just an experiment because i was curious about AI capability. 

to play this experiment: [https://www.pixelfork.ai/publish/db77b355-12db-4f38-934b-9ff01e0b70e1](https://www.pixelfork.ai/publish/db77b355-12db-4f38-934b-9ff01e0b70e1)

comments.author: mallcopsarebastards
comments.body: what do you think "no engine" means in this context?

replies.author: gamesformygirlfriend
replies.body: means this experiment was done without any Traditional engines. like UE, Unity or Godot or any other.

replies.author: mallcopsarebastards
replies.body: the purpose of an engine is so that you don't have to reinvent the wheel on general game dev systems. threejs is a 3d graphics engine and your llm is taking the place of a raycasting engine by reimplementing all the standard functionality you would find in an engine. I guess you can technically say you're not using an engine here but I don't really think that means anything and I don't even think it's a good thing. You'd probably be better off from a performance / maintainability perspective actually using an engine.

comments.author: Alone-Leg-1281
comments.body:
pretty sure this is camera mirroring where you render the scene a second time with the camera flipped under the map. I guess technically its like a single bounce. here is some reference: [https://aras-p.info/texts/obliqueortho.html](https://aras-p.info/texts/obliqueortho.html) . Amenisa the Dark Descent does this for world reflections so its not a new technique. It's also why reflections are avoided doing a whole separate pass on the scene isn't cheap.  
  
webgpu doesn't have access to RT cores so you have to do software based methods. It can be done but it will be very slow. I have some source you can look at these are all software based methods but you can do it on the gpu in the browser. actual ray traced reflections are really expensive a 1920x1080 screen assuming you touch ever pixel will be around 2 million rays. even a moderately powerful card on the market will sweat a little doing this.   

surfel based global illumination: [https://juretriglav.si/surfel-based-global-illumination-on-the-web/](https://juretriglav.si/surfel-based-global-illumination-on-the-web/)   
working bvh demo in webgpu: [https://github.com/AddisonPrairie/WebGPU-LVBH-demo](https://github.com/AddisonPrairie/WebGPU-LVBH-demo)

comments.author: Alone-Leg-1281
comments.body:
There is no raytracing. It's just rendering the scene from the bottom of the map with an oblique view frustum or something of the sort. I guess that is kind of like raytracing but it's probably not what you were thinking. 

 Webgpu doesn't have access to rt cores so you have to solve it in software. there are some samples floating around such as https://juretriglav.si/surfel-based-global-illumination-on-the-web/ . I think you can prompt an agent to solve it in one go just need to frame it correctly with the correct libraries to stitch together.
